fields.Text: When designing a database, {{c1::nouns}} are king: they usually become {{c2::entities or attributes}}.

fields.Front: Define 'entity'.
fields.Back: A single thing that exists with independent existence; any object in the mini-world we want to model and store information about (e.g. Student, Professor, Classroom, Employee).

fields.Front: Define 'attribute'.
fields.Back: Describes a thing; defines the information about an entity that needs to be stored. An entity has 0 or more attributes; each attribute has a domain. E.g. Age, SSN, Sex, Name.

fields.Front: Define 'domain' (value set) of an attribute.
fields.Back: The type/set of values an attribute can take, e.g. string, integer, real, date; more specifically Age: 0-120.

fields.Front: What is the difference between an attribute, its value and its domain?
fields.Back: Attribute: Age. Value: 25 (what one entity holds). Domain: the set of allowed values, e.g. integers 0-120.

fields.Front: What is the difference between an entity type and an entity?
fields.Back: An entity type defines a set of entities with the same attributes (like a class); an entity is one instance of an entity type (like an object).

fields.Front: What is an entity set (collection)?
fields.Back: The group of all entities of one entity type.

fields.Text: A key attribute is one whose values are {{c1::unique}} for every entity, so it {{c2::identifies}} one entity.

fields.Front: Composite vs. simple (atomic) attribute: define and give the slide example.
fields.Back: Composite can be divided into parts with independent meaning (Name = 'Bart Simpson' -> first, last); simple cannot be divided (Age = 45).

fields.Front: Single-valued vs. multi-valued attribute: define and give the slide example.
fields.Back: Single-valued holds exactly one value per entity (Age); multi-valued can hold several (CollegeDegrees).

fields.Front: Derived vs. stored attribute: define and give the slide example.
fields.Back: Derived can be computed from other stored data (Age); stored must be stored (Birthdate).

fields.Text: Slide examples: composite vs simple = {{c1::Bart Simpson vs 45}}; multi-valued vs single-valued = {{c2::CollegeDegrees vs Age}}; derived vs stored = {{c3::Age vs Birthdate}}.

fields.Front: What are the two reasons an attribute value may be null? Give the slide examples.
fields.Back: Not applicable (Apartment Number: some people have none) and not known (Phone Number: the person has one but we do not know it).

fields.Text: A null Apartment Number is an example of a value that is {{c1::not applicable}}; a null Phone Number is an example of a value that is {{c2::not known}}.

fields.Front: What are the domains of Age, Name and Cost (speaker-note answers)?
fields.Back: Speaker notes: Age 0-120; Name alphabetic characters (possibly restricted length); Cost 0.00 to some upper limit (real). In the video: age = integers greater than 0 (or 0 to 114); name = characters/strings; cost = real numbers.

fields.Front: In Chen notation, how are these drawn: entity type, attribute, key attribute?
fields.Back: Entity type: rectangle. Attribute: oval. Key attribute: oval with the name underlined.

fields.Front: In Chen notation, how are these drawn: multi-valued attribute, composite attribute, derived attribute?
fields.Back: Multi-valued: double oval. Composite: oval with component ovals attached. Derived: dashed oval.

fields.Text: Chen notation: a multi-valued attribute is a {{c1::double oval}}, a derived attribute is a {{c2::dashed oval}}, a key attribute is {{c3::underlined}}.

fields.Front: Instructor: what is the difference between the nouns 'employee' and 'salary' in the case study?
fields.Back: Employee is a thing that has existence, so it is an entity; salary describes the employee ($40,000 describes Homer Simpson), so it is an attribute.

fields.Front: Which noun in the case study is only implied, and where does it end up?
fields.Back: Date ('keep track of when the employee started managing'); it becomes the StartDate attribute on the MANAGES relationship.

fields.Text: Store {{c1::Birthdate}} rather than {{c2::Age}}: if you stored the latter, every time it changed you would have to recalculate it.

fields.Front: What is the instructor's test for whether an attribute like Name is composite?
fields.Back: Whether there are parts you might need to get at (e.g. just the first name). Breaking a first name into letters makes no sense, so FirstName is simple.

fields.Text: Instructor's domain example: a Western student number is over the domain of {{c1::nine digits}}.

fields.Front: What keys does the instructor give for a student and for a patient, and why is a key needed?
fields.Back: Student number or Western user ID; OHIP number. Because two students could both be named Homer Simpson.

fields.Text: 'I tend to not say entity type, I tend to just call it an {{c1::entity}}'; strictly, an entity is an {{c2::instance}} of an entity type.

fields.Front: Are derived attributes always drawn on an ER diagram?
fields.Back: No: 'if you even want to show it, you don't always show it'; generally only stored attributes are shown.

fields.Front: In draw.io, which shapes does the instructor use for an entity, an ordinary attribute and a multi-valued attribute?
fields.Back: Rectangle for the entity; the plain oval under General for ordinary attributes; the Entity Relation library's double-ring attribute only for multi-valued attributes.

fields.Text: 'Most of the time entities don't have {{c1::two unique keys}}', but DEPARTMENT does ({{c2::Name and Number}}).

fields.Front: What is the instructor's example of an entity taking different values for the same attributes?
fields.Back: Homer Simpson and Marge Simpson are two entities of the same type; Marge's name and other attribute values differ from Homer's.
